passage.preamble: Scrooge is a cold, mean old man who lives by himself in a big, dark set of rooms in London. It is Christmas Eve, and he has just come home through the fog.

numberedLines.text: Now, it is a fact, that there was nothing at all particular about the knocker on the
door, except that it was very large. It is also a fact, that Scrooge had seen it, night
and morning, during his whole residence in that place; also that Scrooge had as little
of what is called fancy about him as any man in the city of London, even including--
which is a bold word--the corporation, aldermen, and livery. Let it also be borne in
mind that Scrooge had not bestowed one thought on Marley, since his last mention of his
seven years' dead partner that afternoon. And then let any man explain to me, if he can,
how it happened that Scrooge, having his key in the lock of the door, saw in the
knocker, without its undergoing any intermediate process of change--not a knocker, but
Marley's face.
Marley's face. It was not in impenetrable shadow as the other objects in the yard were,
but had a dismal light about it, like a bad lobster in a dark cellar. It was not angry
or ferocious, but looked at Scrooge as Marley used to look: with ghostly spectacles
turned up on its ghostly forehead. The hair was curiously stirred, as if by breath or
hot air; and, though the eyes were wide open, they were perfectly motionless. That, and
its livid colour, made it horrible; but its horror seemed to be in spite of the face and
beyond its control, rather than a part of its own expression.
As Scrooge looked fixedly at this phenomenon, it was a knocker again.
To say that he was not startled, or that his blood was not conscious of a terrible
sensation to which it had been a stranger from infancy, would be untrue. But he put his
hand upon the key he had relinquished, turned it sturdily, walked in, and lighted his
candle.
He did pause, with a moment's irresolution, before he shut the door; and he did look
cautiously behind it first, as if he half expected to be terrified with the sight of
Marley's pigtail sticking out into the hall. But there was nothing on the back of the
door, except the screws and nuts that held the knocker on, so he said "Pooh, pooh!" and
closed it with a bang.
The sound resounded through the house like thunder. Every room above, and every cask in
the wine-merchant's cellars below, appeared to have a separate peal of echoes of its
own. Scrooge was not a man to be frightened by echoes. He fastened the door, and walked
across the hall, and up the stairs; slowly too: trimming his candle as he went.
Sitting-room, bedroom, lumber-room. All as they should be. Nobody under the table,
nobody under the sofa; a small fire in the grate; spoon and basin ready; and the little
saucepan of gruel (Scrooge had a cold in his head) upon the hob. Nobody under the bed;
nobody in the closet; nobody in his dressing-gown, which was hanging up in a suspicious
attitude against the wall. Lumber-room as usual. Old fire-guard, old shoes, two fish-
baskets, washing-stand on three legs, and a poker.
Quite satisfied, he closed his door, and locked himself in; double-locked himself in,
which was not his custom. Thus secured against surprise, he took off his cravat; put on
his dressing-gown and slippers, and his nightcap; and sat down before the fire to take
his gruel.
It was a very low fire indeed; nothing on such a bitter night. He was obliged to sit
close to it, and brood over it, before he could extract the least sensation of warmth
from such a handful of fuel. The fireplace was an old one, built by some Dutch merchant
long ago, and paved all round with quaint Dutch tiles, designed to illustrate the
Scriptures. There were Cains and Abels, Pharaoh's daughters; Queens of Sheba, Angelic
messengers descending through the air on clouds like feather-beds, Abrahams,
Belshazzars, Apostles putting off to sea in butter-boats, hundreds of figures to attract
his thoughts; and yet that face of Marley, seven years dead, came like the ancient
Prophet's rod, and swallowed up the whole. If each smooth tile had been a blank at
first, with power to shape some picture on its surface from the disjointed fragments of
his thoughts, there would have been a copy of old Marley's head on every one.
"Humbug!" said Scrooge; and walked across the room.
After several turns, he sat down again. As he threw his head back in the chair, his
glance happened to rest upon a bell, a disused bell, that hung in the room, and
communicated for some purpose now forgotten with a chamber in the highest story of the
building. It was with great astonishment, and with a strange, inexplicable dread, that
as he looked, he saw this bell begin to swing. It swung so softly in the outset that it
scarcely made a sound; but soon it rang out loudly, and so did every bell in the house.
This might have lasted half a minute, or a minute, but it seemed an hour. The bells
ceased as they had begun, together. They were succeeded by a clanking noise, deep down
below; as if some person were dragging a heavy chain over the casks in the wine-
merchant's cellar. Scrooge then remembered to have heard that ghosts in haunted houses
were described as dragging chains.
The cellar-door flew open with a booming sound, and then he heard the noise much louder,
on the floors below; then coming up the stairs; then coming straight towards his door.
"It's humbug still!" said Scrooge. "I won't believe it."
His colour changed though, when, without a pause, it came on through the heavy door, and
passed into the room before his eyes. Upon its coming in, the dying flame leaped up, as
though it cried, "I know him; Marley's Ghost!" and fell again.
The same face: the very same. Marley in his pigtail, usual waistcoat, tights and boots;
the tassels on the latter bristling, like his pigtail, and his coat-skirts, and the hair
upon his head. The chain he drew was clasped about his middle. It was long, and wound
about him like a tail; and it was made (for Scrooge observed it closely) of cash-boxes,
keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel. His body was
transparent; so that Scrooge, observing him, and looking through his waistcoat, could
see the two buttons on his coat behind.
"How now!" said Scrooge, caustic and cold as ever. "What do you want with me?"
"Much!"--Marley's voice, no doubt about it.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 5. What was the one odd thing about the knocker?

rows.key: The very great size of the thing itself.

options.value: The very great size of the thing itself.
Scrooge had seen it night and morning.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at lines 2 and 3, and it says how often he saw it rather than what was odd.

options.value: The thing had hung there for many years.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Likely for an old house; lines 1 to 5 never say it.

options.value: It had as little fancy about it as any man.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Line 3 and line 4 give that want of fancy to Scrooge, not to the knocker.

rows.hintCore: Check who each answer is about before you pick one.
rows.walkScript: Line 1 says there was nothing at all particular about the knocker. The same line gives the one exception: it was very large. How often he saw it comes next, at line 2.

stem.text: Look at lines 6 to 10. What had Scrooge not done since that afternoon?

rows.key: Given Marley so much as one thought.

options.value: He had thought about Marley all day.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Line 6 says he had not bestowed one thought on Marley.

options.value: Given Marley so much as one thought.
Put his key into the lock of the door.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at line 8, and it is what he was doing rather than what he had not done.

options.value: Gone up to look at his partner's old rooms.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Likely enough on such a night; lines 6 to 10 never say it.

rows.hintCore: One of these turns a not into a yes.
rows.walkScript: Line 6 says he had not bestowed one thought on Marley. Line 7 dates that from his last mention of him that afternoon. The key at line 8 is what he was doing, not what he missed.

stem.text: Look at lines 11 to 17. What made the face horrible to look at?

rows.key: The still open eyes and the awful colour.

options.value: It looked angry and fierce at him.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Lines 12 and 13 say it was not angry or ferocious.

options.value: It had a dismal light, like a bad lobster.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses line 12 and names how it looked rather than what made it horrible.

options.value: The still open eyes and the awful colour.
The hair was stirred as if by hot air.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at line 14, and line 15 attaches the horror to the eyes and the colour.

rows.hintCore: The passage says it was not one of these. Find that one.
rows.walkScript: Line 15 says the eyes were wide open and perfectly motionless. The same line says That, and its livid colour, made it horrible. That points back to the still open eyes, not to the hair.

stem.text: Look at lines 19 to 22. What did Scrooge do after the shock?

rows.key: He turned his key and he walked in.

options.value: The sight left him quite unmoved.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Lines 19 and 20 say it would be untrue to say he was not startled.

options.value: He let go of the key he was holding.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at line 20, and it is what he had already done rather than what came next.

options.value: He lighted his candle, then turned the key.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: Line 21 turns the key before line 22 lights the candle, so this reverses them.

options.value: He turned his key and he walked in.

rows.hintCore: Two of these happened. Ask which one came next.
rows.walkScript: Line 20 says he put his hand upon the key he had let go. Line 21 says he turned it sturdily and walked in. The candle at line 22 comes after both.

stem.text: Look at lines 23 to 27. What does 'irresolution' on line 23 mean here?

rows.key: A moment of not knowing what to do.

options.value: A moment of not knowing what to do.
A promise that he had not kept.
options.tagChildHint: The parts of a word do not always add up. Check the whole word in the sentence.
options.execution: Takes the meaning from resolution, a word it holds inside it.

options.value: A sudden rush of panic at the door.
options.tagChildHint: Pick the word you can prove from the text. Close is not the same.
options.execution: An adjacent state; line 23 gives a moment of hanging back rather than panic.

options.value: A careful look behind the open door.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at lines 23 and 24, and it is what he did rather than what the word means.

rows.hintCore: Ask whether the word names a deed or a state.
rows.walkScript: Line 23 says he did pause, with a moment of it, before he shut the door. Line 24 says he looked cautiously behind it first. So the word names the hanging back, not the looking.

stem.text: Look at lines 28 to 31 and 60 to 66. What does the second noise do that the first does not?

rows.key: The first noise he leaves behind, and the second one follows him.

options.value: The first is like thunder, and the second is like a dragged chain.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses lines 28 and 62, and names each sound rather than what changes between them.

options.value: The first noise he leaves behind, and the second one follows him.
The bells ring first, and the door bangs a long while after.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: Line 27 bangs the door before line 59 rings the bells, so this turns the order round.

options.value: The flame leaps up first, and then it falls again in the grate.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: True at line 69 and line 70, outside both windows; neither window has a flame in it. In the window, line 30 answers the stem: 'own. Scrooge was not a man to be frightened'.

rows.hintCore: Two of these only list the noises.
rows.walkScript: Line 30 says he was not a man to be frightened by echoes. Lines 65 and 66 have the noise come up the stairs and straight to his door. One he leaves behind him, the other comes to find him.

stem.text: Look at lines 32 to 37. What is Scrooge doing in these lines?

rows.key: Looking in every place a person could hide.

options.value: Finding all the rooms in order, just as before.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses line 32 and repeats his verdict rather than what he is doing to reach it.

options.value: Noting the gruel standing ready on the hob.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at lines 33 and 34, and it is one item on the list rather than the point of it.

options.value: Looking in every place a person could hide.
Making sure the servants have all gone home.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A plausible reason to walk the rooms; lines 32 to 37 never give it.

rows.hintCore: Take the whole list, not one thing off it.
rows.walkScript: Line 32 lists the rooms and then starts on the places. Lines 33 to 35 give under the table, under the sofa, in the closet. Every one of them is a place a person could be.

stem.text: Look at lines 38 to 41. What shows that the face has shaken him?

rows.key: He turned the lock a second time, which was new.

options.value: He was quite satisfied, and so he closed his door.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses line 38 and repeats his own verdict rather than the sign against it.

options.value: He put on his dressing-gown and his nightcap.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at lines 39 and 40, and it is his usual habit rather than a broken one.

options.value: Double-locking the door was his usual custom.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Line 39 says it was not his custom.

options.value: He turned the lock a second time, which was new.

rows.hintCore: One of these says it was his custom. Line 39 does not.
rows.walkScript: Line 38 says he double-locked himself in. Line 39 adds that this was not his custom. The gown and the nightcap are what he does every night.

stem.text: Look at lines 54 to 59. Why is the swinging bell so strange?

rows.key: Nobody has used that bell for a long time.

options.value: Nobody has used that bell for a long time.
It rang out loudly, and every bell rang too.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at line 59, and it is what followed rather than why the swinging is strange.

options.value: He felt a strange dread that he could not explain.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses line 57 and names his feeling rather than the reason for it.

options.value: The wind had got into the rooms above him.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A real explanation for a swinging bell; lines 54 to 59 never give it.

rows.hintCore: A draught would explain it. Check whether the lines give one.
rows.walkScript: Line 55 calls it a disused bell. Lines 55 and 56 say it went to a chamber whose purpose is now forgotten. So nothing up there can be pulling on it.

stem.text: Look at lines 68 to 70. What did the flame do as the ghost came in?

rows.key: It leaped up and then fell back again.

options.value: It came on through the heavy door.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Line 68 gives that to the ghost, not to the flame.

options.value: It leaped up and then fell back again.
It called out that it knew Marley.
options.tagChildHint: Figures of speech are not facts. Ask what the words are really saying.
options.execution: Line 70 says as though it cried, so the flame is given a voice it does not have.

options.value: Scrooge changed colour as the thing passed.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at line 68, and it is Scrooge who changes colour rather than the flame.

rows.hintCore: Before you give the flame a voice, check whether it has one.
rows.walkScript: Line 69 says the dying flame leaped up as it came in. Line 70 says it fell again straight after. The words in the middle are what the leap seemed to say.

stem.text: Look at lines 78 and 79. What does 'caustic' on line 78 mean here?

rows.key: Sharp and cutting in what he says.

options.value: Able to burn like a strong acid.
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: The commonest everyday sense of the word; line 78 puts it on how he speaks.

options.value: Careful about every word he uses.
options.tagChildHint: The parts of a word do not always add up. Check the whole word in the sentence.
options.execution: Takes the meaning from cautious, a word it resembles in form.

options.value: Sharp and cutting in what he says.
Cold, in the way he had always been.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at line 78, and it names the other half of the pair rather than this word.

rows.hintCore: The line gives two words for one voice. One of them is cold.
rows.walkScript: Line 78 says he spoke, and gives two words for how. One of them is cold, so the other one is doing different work. His question to the ghost is short and sharp, which is the other word.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. What does Scrooge keep doing after he sees the face?

rows.key: He says he is not frightened, but he checks the whole house.

options.value: He says Pooh, pooh, and then a little later he says Humbug too.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses lines 26 and 53 and quotes him twice rather than naming anything he does.

options.value: He says he is not frightened, but he checks the whole house.
He is bold at the start, but his nerve does not last.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A tidy shape the passage never carries: line 78 still has him caustic and cold.

options.value: He fears the thing, so he sends for help to sit up.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A plausible course for a frightened man; he is alone throughout and asks no one.

rows.hintCore: Before you answer, look right through and count what he actually does.
rows.walkScript: At line 24 he looks behind the door before he will shut it. At line 35 he is looking in the closet and under the bed. At line 67 he says it is humbug still, and will not believe it.
